subject: CREATIVE ARTS
title: Songs
overview: Songs carry words, tunes and feelings. In this sub-strand you will sing sacred, patriotic and topical songs with the right notes, beat, speed and volume, and with clear words, gestures and facial expressions. You will learn the East African Community Anthem in unison, then identify and perform Kenyan folk songs and sort them by the occasion they belong to.

lessons.title: Sacred, patriotic and topical songs
objectives: Tell sacred, patriotic and topical songs apart.
State the message and mood of a song you listen to.
Choose a fitting way to stand and look while each type is sung.
lessons.intro: Before a choir sings, the singers need to know what kind of song is in front of them. A prayer, a song of love for one’s country and a song about washing hands are not performed in the same way.
lessons.notes:
A song is music with words and a tune. In this sub-strand you sing three kinds of song with care, and later you sing folk songs as well.

### Sacred songs
A sacred song is used for worship and prayer. Hymns and other songs of praise sung in a church, at the mosque, or in a school assembly when the class is praying, are sacred songs. The mood is respectful and calm. The face is peaceful. The voice is clear but not shouted. You stand or sit as your community and your teacher expect during worship.

### Patriotic songs
A patriotic song shows love for your country or for the East African community of countries. The Kenya National Anthem and the East African Community Anthem are patriotic songs. You stand tall and still. You sing with pride, and you do not talk, laugh or walk about while the anthem is sung.

### Topical songs
A topical song is about a theme in daily life. The topic might be clean hands, a tidy compound, crossing the road or caring for trees. The words teach a message, so every word must be heard. The mood follows the message: a song about a happy clean-up can be bright; a song that warns about danger can be firmer.

When you listen, ask three questions. Is this song sacred, patriotic or topical? What is it telling people to do or to feel? What should my face and my body show while I sing it?

Here is a short topical song you may sing:

Wash your hands, wash your hands,
Before you eat and after play.
Wash your hands, wash your hands,
Soap and water keep germs away.

Sing it lightly, with a smile, and mime washing so the message is seen as well as heard.

keyWords.meaning: a song used for worship and prayer
a song that shows love for one’s country or region
a song about a theme in daily life
the feeling a song carries, such as calm, proud or cheerful

examples.problem: The class sings a song that asks learners to plant trees. Which type of song is it?
steps: It is about a daily-life theme, not worship and not the nation.
Songs about a theme are topical.

examples.problem: During the Kenya National Anthem, a learner walks to the door. What should the learner do instead?
steps: The national anthem is a patriotic song.
Listeners and singers stand still until it ends.
examples.answer: Stand still until the anthem ends.

activity.title: Listen and name the type
materials: Recordings of a sacred song, a patriotic song and a topical song
steps: Listen to three short songs chosen by the teacher.
For each song, write whether it is sacred, patriotic or topical, and write its message in one sentence.
Show with your face and hands the mood of each song without making a sound.
Sing the handwashing song together, adding the washing gesture.
Discuss which mood fitted which song.

practice.question: What is a sacred song?
practice.answer: A song used for worship and prayer.

practice.question: Give one example of a patriotic song.
practice.answer: The Kenya National Anthem or the East African Community Anthem.

practice.question: What question helps you find the message of a topical song?
practice.answer: What is the song telling people to do or to remember?

summary: Sacred songs are for worship, patriotic songs show love of country, and topical songs teach a daily message.
The mood of the face and body should match the song.
Stand still for an anthem.

lessons.title: Singing the right notes and the right beat
objectives: Explain pitch and rhythm in singing.
Match a simple tune and keep a steady beat.
Hear when a note is too high, too low or late.
lessons.intro: Two people can know the same words and still sing two different songs if one is on the wrong notes or ahead of the beat. Accuracy is what makes a group sound like one voice.
lessons.notes:
Good singing starts with two musical skills: pitch and rhythm.

### Pitch
Pitch is how high or low a note is. A tune is a line of pitches. If you sing a note higher or lower than the tune, you are out of tune. To find the pitch:

- Listen to the starting note before you sing. A teacher, a keyboard, a chime or a recorder can give it.
- Hum the note quietly, then sing the word on that same note.
- Keep your ears open while you sing. If the class sounds as if it is splitting into two tunes, stop and take the starting note again.
- Do not shout. Shouting pushes the pitch up and makes the voice harsh.

### Rhythm
Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds, and the beat is the steady pulse underneath. Clap the beat first. Then speak the words in time with the claps. Only then sing.

A useful order is: listen, clap the beat, speak the words in time, sing.

### Staying together
Watch the person leading the song. Breathe before the first word, not in the middle of a short line if you can help it. If you finish a line early, you are rushing. If you are still singing when others have stopped, you are dragging. Both mistakes spoil the rhythm.

Try the handwashing song again. Clap once for each word-beat: “Wash (clap) your (clap) hands (clap)”. Then sing it on a tune the teacher gives you, all on the same beat. Accuracy means the notes match the tune and the words sit on the beat.

keyWords.meaning: how high or low a note is
a line of notes that makes the melody of a song
the pattern of long and short sounds
the steady pulse you can clap to

examples.problem: The class starts a song and some voices are much higher than the leader. What skill needs work?
steps: High and low are about pitch.
Matching the leader’s notes is singing in tune.
examples.answer: Pitch. They should take the starting note again and match it.

examples.problem: A group claps four steady beats in a line. How many claps are in two lines?

activity.title: Clap, speak, then sing
materials: A pitching instrument if the school has one, such as a recorder or keyboard
steps: The leader plays or sings the first note. Everyone hums it.
Clap a steady beat while speaking the words.
Sing the song, listening for voices that rush or sing a different tune.
Stop, fix one problem, and sing the line again.
Tell your partner whether you were listening to pitch or to the beat.

practice.question: What is pitch?
practice.answer: How high or low a note is.

practice.question: What should you do before singing the first word?
practice.answer: Listen to the starting note and breathe.

practice.question: What is the difference between rushing and dragging?
practice.answer: Rushing is finishing too early. Dragging is still singing after the beat has moved on.

summary: Pitch is high and low. Rhythm is the pattern of the beat.
Listen, clap, speak, then sing.
Shouting and rushing both spoil accuracy.

lessons.title: Tempo, dynamics and the mood of a song
objectives: Follow a fast or slow tempo and a loud or soft dynamic.
Show the mood of a song with the voice.
Explain why the same song can feel different if the speed or volume changes.
lessons.intro: A lullaby sung at marching speed stops being a lullaby. Speed and volume are instructions. Singers follow them so the feeling of the song stays true.
lessons.notes:
Performance directions tell singers how to perform, not only which words to sing. Two directions you use in Grade 4 are tempo and dynamics.

### Tempo
Tempo is the speed of the beat. A fast tempo can feel excited, playful or urgent. A slow tempo can feel calm, sad, serious or grand. Patriotic songs are often sung at a steady walking tempo, not a race. A topical song about play might be quicker. You do not choose the tempo by yourself in a group. The leader sets it, and everyone stays with it.

### Dynamics
Dynamics means how loud or soft the singing is. Soft singing can show gentleness, a secret or a prayer. Louder singing can show joy, a warning or a call to stand together. Louder is not the same as shouting. You still sing the correct pitch. A simple pattern is to sing one verse softly and the next a little louder, if the leader asks for that contrast.

### Mood
Mood is the feeling. Talk about the words before you sing. A song about a funeral is not sung with a grin and a skip. A marriage song is not sung as if the class were bored. After you know the message, choose the tempo, the dynamics and the face that carry that message.

Try one line of a song you know in three ways: slow and soft, moderate and clear, fast and louder. Then decide which way matches the words. The matching way is the one you keep.

keyWords.meaning: the speed of the music
how loud or soft the music is
instructions about speed, volume and expression

examples.problem: A prayerful sacred song is sung very fast and very loud. What is wrong?
steps: Sacred songs usually need a calm mood.
Fast and shouted singing does not match a prayer.
examples.answer: The tempo and dynamics do not match the mood. It should be slower and gentler, without shouting.

examples.problem: The leader asks for a soft first line and a louder second line. Which direction is this?
steps: Loud and soft are dynamics.
Speed would be tempo.

activity.title: Same words, different directions
materials: Two cards labelled Fast/Slow and Loud/Soft
steps: Sing a short song at the tempo the teacher sets.
Sing it again much slower, then a little faster, and discuss which speed matches the words.
Sing one line softly and the next more loudly, still in tune.
In groups, choose the mood of the song and show it with your voices.
Explain your choice to another group.

practice.question: What is tempo?
practice.answer: The speed of the beat.

practice.question: What are dynamics?
practice.answer: How loud or soft the singing is.

practice.question: Why should you not shout when a song asks to be loud?
practice.answer: Shouting spoils the pitch and makes the voice harsh.

summary: Tempo is speed. Dynamics are loud and soft.
The leader sets the directions and the group follows.
Mood, speed and volume should match the message.

lessons.title: Gestures, facial expression and diction
objectives: Use gestures and facial expression that match a song.
Sing with clear diction so the words are understood.
Keep performance etiquette while singing with others.
lessons.intro: An audience that cannot hear the words cannot receive the message. The face, the hands and the clarity of speech finish the work that pitch and rhythm began.
lessons.notes:
Performance technique is the way you use your body and your voice. Performance etiquette is the polite behaviour that belongs with singing.

### Gestures
A gesture is a movement of the hands, arms or body that shows the meaning. Washing hands, holding them over the heart for love of country, or opening the arms for welcome are gestures. Gestures should be big enough to see and slow enough to match the beat. They should not hit the person beside you. If a sacred song is sung in a still, respectful way, do not add playful dances.

### Facial expression
Your face tells the mood before the words do. A bright topical song needs lively eyes. A serious patriotic song needs a steady, proud face. A sad song needs a quiet face. Practise in pairs so you can see if your face matches what you claim to be singing.

### Diction
Diction is the clear speaking of words inside the song. Open the mouth, sound the ends of words, and do not mumble. If the song is in an indigenous language, learn the words from someone who speaks that language. Do not guess the pronunciation and then laugh at it. Clear diction lets the message travel.

### Etiquette
- Stand or sit as the group agreed.
- Face the audience.
- Do not talk, chew or nudge others while singing.
- Start and stop with the leader.
- Bow or smile once at the end if that is the group’s custom, then stand still.
- Listen to other groups as carefully as you want them to listen to you.

Good singing involves accurate pitch and rhythm, the right tempo and dynamics, clear diction, and gestures and faces that carry the message, all done with respect.

keyWords.meaning: a movement that shows the meaning of the song
clear pronunciation of the words
polite behaviour expected during a performance
the look on the face that shows feeling

examples.problem: A topical song says “sweep the compound”, but the singers only stand with their hands in their pockets. What could they add?
steps: The words describe an action.
A gesture can show that action.
examples.answer: A sweeping gesture that matches the beat.

examples.problem: The audience cannot tell what the last words of each line are. Which skill needs practice?
steps: Unclear word endings are a diction problem.

activity.title: Message on the face and in the hands
materials: The handwashing song or another short topical song
Space to stand in a group
steps: Speak the words slowly, making the ends of the words clear.
Agree on one gesture for the main action in the song.
Sing with the gesture, the matching face, and a steady beat.
Another group watches and says whether the message was clear.
Thank the watchers and listen to their song in silence.

practice.question: What is diction?
practice.answer: Clear pronunciation of the words in a song.

practice.question: Give two rules of singing etiquette.
practice.answer: Any two: do not talk while singing, face the audience, start and stop with the leader, listen to other groups, do not nudge others.

practice.question: What does good singing involve?
practice.answer: Accurate pitch and rhythm, suitable tempo and dynamics, clear diction, and gestures and facial expressions that match the message.

summary: Gestures and faces show the message.
Diction keeps the words clear.
Etiquette means the group is respectful to the song and the audience.

lessons.title: Words and meaning of the East African Community Anthem
objectives: Say what the East African Community Anthem is for.
Speak the first verse and the chorus with correct words.
Explain the message of unity, peace and hard work.
lessons.intro: Kenya belongs to a family of countries called the East African Community. That family has its own anthem, sung in Kiswahili, which Kenyan schools learn alongside the Kenya National Anthem.
lessons.notes:
The East African Community Anthem is called Wimbo wa Jumuiya Afrika Mashariki. It is a patriotic song for the region. It was adopted in 2010. It has three verses and a chorus, and it is sung in unison when a group performs it together: everyone sings the same tune at the same time.

Learn the first verse and the chorus first. Speak them before you sing them.

**Verse 1**
Ee Mungu twaomba ulinde
Jumuiya Afrika Mashariki
Tuwezeshe kuishi kwa amani
Tutimize na malengo yetu.

This verse is a prayer. It asks God to guard the East African Community, to help the people live in peace, and to help them fulfil their aims.

**Chorus**
Jumuiya Yetu sote tuilinde
Tuwajibike tuimarike
Umoja wetu ni nguzo yetu
Idumu Jumuiya yetu.

The chorus says: let us all guard our Community, be responsible and grow strong. Our unity is our pillar. May our Community last.

**The other verses, in meaning**
Verse 2 says patriotism and solidarity should be the foundation of unity, and that the people should guard freedom, peace, culture and customs.
Verse 3 says people should work carefully in industries and on farms, give their effort and their resources, and build a better Community.

The whole anthem values peace, unity, responsibility, patriotism and hard work. You will sing verse 1 and the chorus together in the next lesson. Stand tall when you practise the words, because the meaning is serious even while you are still only speaking.

keyWords.meaning: an official song of a country or a community of countries
everyone singing the same tune at the same time
the part of a song that returns after the verses
being together as one

examples.problem: Which line asks that the people may live in peace?
steps: Look at verse 1.
“Tuwezeshe kuishi kwa amani” is about living in peace.

examples.problem: The anthem has 3 verses. You are learning verse 1 now. How many verses are still to learn later?

activity.title: Internalise the words
materials: A recording or a live performance of the anthem
The words written on the board
steps: Listen to verse 1 and the chorus without singing.
Discuss in pairs what the verse asks for.
Speak the words together, slowly and clearly.
Cover the board and say as much as you can remember.
Check any word you missed and say that line again.

practice.question: In which language is the East African Community Anthem sung?
practice.answer: Kiswahili.

practice.question: What does singing in unison mean?
practice.answer: Everyone sings the same tune at the same time.

practice.question: Give two values found in the anthem.
practice.answer: Any two: peace, unity, responsibility, patriotism, hard work.

practice.question: What does the chorus say our unity is?
practice.answer: Our pillar (nguzo).

summary: The anthem is a Kiswahili patriotic song of the East African Community.
Verse 1 is a prayer for protection, peace and fulfilled aims.
The chorus calls for unity, responsibility and a lasting Community.

lessons.title: Singing the East African Community Anthem in unison
objectives: Sing verse 1 and the chorus together on one tune.
Keep performance etiquette for an anthem.
Explain why the class sings it with respect.
lessons.intro: Speaking the words was the first half of the work. Singing them in unison means every voice joins the same tune, starts together and stops together.
lessons.notes:
Unison singing fails if people begin on different notes or treat an anthem like playground noise. Use the skills you already have.

### How to practise
1. Stand still, feet slightly apart, arms at your sides, eyes forward.
2. Listen to the whole of verse 1 and the chorus.
3. Hum the first note after the leader gives it.
4. Sing one line, then stop and repair any wrong word or late voice.
5. Join the lines. Breathe at the ends of lines.
6. Add the chorus. Keep the tempo steady. Do not speed up as you become excited.
7. Sing verse 1 and the chorus once through without stopping.

### Etiquette for this anthem
- Stand for the whole anthem.
- Do not talk, laugh or conduct your friends.
- Use a proud, calm face. A hand-on-heart gesture may be used if the teacher asks for it. Do not add dances.
- Diction matters because the anthem is in Kiswahili. Sound each word: Ju-mui-ya, tu-wa-ji-bi-ke, u-mo-ja.
- If you forget a word, keep the tune quietly and come back in. Do not shout a guess.

### Why it is worth singing well
The anthem asks East Africans to live in peace and to guard their unity. Singing it with care is an act of patriotism and of respect for neighbouring countries as well as for Kenya. When the class sings in unison, the sound itself demonstrates the unity the words describe.

Later you can add verses 2 and 3. Verse 2 is about patriotism, solidarity, freedom, peace and culture. Verse 3 is about careful work in industries and on farms. Do not rush to them until verse 1 and the chorus are accurate.

keyWords.meaning: all voices on the same tune together
standing together with other people

examples.problem: Half the class starts before the leader’s hand comes down. What rule have they broken?
steps: Unison needs one start.
The leader shows the start.
examples.answer: They did not start together with the leader.

examples.problem: A singer dances during the chorus. Why is that poor etiquette here?
steps: An anthem is sung standing still.
Dancing changes a serious patriotic song into something else.
examples.answer: The anthem is performed standing still, with a calm proud face, not as a dance.

activity.title: Unison practice
steps: Listen once, then hum the opening note together.
Sing verse 1 in unison, repairing one line if the pitch splits.
Add the chorus at a steady tempo.
A small group listens and comments on diction and whether everyone started together.
Sing once more with full etiquette: still bodies, calm faces, no talking.

practice.question: What should you do just before the first word of the anthem?
practice.answer: Stand still, listen, and hum or hear the starting note.

practice.question: Why is unison a good match for the message of this anthem?
practice.answer: Everyone sings the same tune together, which shows the unity the words ask for.

practice.question: Name two etiquette rules for singing the anthem.
practice.answer: Any two: stand still, do not talk or laugh, use a calm proud face, follow the leader, keep the diction clear.

summary: Take one starting note and sing the same tune together.
Stand still, with clear Kiswahili diction and a steady tempo.
The performance itself is a sign of unity and respect.

lessons.title: Kenyan folk songs: name, community and type
objectives: Identify a folk song by its name and the community that performs it.
Classify folk songs as work, funeral, naming, initiation, marriage or worship songs.
Explain how to find the type when you are not sure.
lessons.intro: A drum can tell you that a celebration is near, but it cannot by itself tell you whether the song is for a wedding, a naming or worship. You have to ask what the song is called, who sings it, and on what occasion.
lessons.notes:
A folk song is a song of a community, passed on by singing rather than invented for one pop concert. Indigenous Kenyan folk songs belong to the communities of this country. When you meet one, record three facts: the **name** of the song or dance-song, the **community**, and the **occasion**.

### Six types, by occasion
- **Work songs** are sung while people dig, grind, herd, paddle or do other shared work. The beat often matches the movement.
- **Funeral songs** are sung to mourn and to comfort a family. They are usually slower and solemn.
- **Naming songs** are sung when a child is given a name. They are joyful.
- **Initiation songs** belong to ceremonies that mark young people moving into a new stage of life in that community. Treat them with respect. Perform at school only the songs a teacher or community member says are suitable for class.
- **Marriage songs** are sung at weddings to celebrate, advise and welcome.
- **Worship songs** are sung in praise or during traditional worship.

### How to classify
Do not guess from the drums alone. Ask: When is this song sung? Match that occasion to the list. Some famous performances are used at more than one joyful event. Say so, instead of forcing one label.

Examples you can identify by name and community:
- **Isukuti** is drum music and dance of Luhya communities, especially the Isukha and Idakho, performed at joyful gatherings such as weddings.
- **Sengenya** is a dance-song of the Mijikenda communities of the Coast, performed at celebrations.
- **Mwomboko** is a dance of the Agikuyu, performed at celebrations including weddings.

Your own community has its own names. Ask an elder or a teacher, and write the name, the community and the occasion in your book. That is identification.

keyWords.meaning: a song of a community, learned by people singing it to one another
the event at which a song is performed
to sort into groups

examples.problem: Women sing a steady song while they grind grain. Which type is it?
steps: The singing happens during work.
Work songs match the movement of the job.

examples.problem: A song is called isukuti and comes from the Isukha and Idakho. Which community group is that?
steps: Isukha and Idakho are Luhya communities.

activity.title: Watch, name and classify
materials: Recordings or a visit from a resource person
A table with columns: Name, Community, Occasion, Type
steps: Watch or listen to two folk songs from different Kenyan communities.
Fill the table for each song.
Classify each one using the six occasions. If it fits more than one joyful event, say so.
Add one song from your own community if someone in the class can name it accurately.
Compare tables with another group and correct any guess that has no occasion to support it.

practice.question: What three facts do you record when you identify a folk song?
practice.answer: Its name, the community, and the occasion.

practice.question: Which type of folk song is sung while people do a shared job?
practice.answer: A work song.

practice.question: Why should initiation songs be chosen carefully for class?
practice.answer: Some belong to community ceremonies and should be performed at school only if a teacher or community member says they are suitable.

practice.question: Name one Kenyan folk dance-song and its community.
practice.answer: Any one accurate pair: isukuti (Luhya, especially Isukha and Idakho), sengenya (Mijikenda), or mwomboko (Agikuyu).

summary: Identify a folk song by name, community and occasion.
Classify it as work, funeral, naming, initiation, marriage or worship.
Do not guess the type from the instruments alone.

lessons.title: Performing a Kenyan folk song
objectives: Take a role in a folk song: soloist, singer or instrumentalist.
Apply pitch, rhythm, diction, gestures and etiquette.
Explain why songs from different Kenyan communities are worth performing.
lessons.intro: Identifying a folk song is listening. Performing it is taking a role and carrying the song with respect for the community it comes from.
lessons.notes:
Choose one school-appropriate indigenous Kenyan folk song. It may come from your community or from another Kenyan community your teacher can teach accurately. Do not invent words. If nobody knows a song well enough, learn a short, suitable one from a recording or a resource person, then perform that.

### Roles
- The **soloist** sings the leading line.
- The **singers** answer or join in.
- The **instrumentalist** keeps the beat on a drum, kayamba, shaker or clapping.
- Everyone uses the performance techniques you have learnt: accurate pitch, steady rhythm, suitable tempo and dynamics, clear diction, and gestures and faces that match the occasion.

Rotate the roles so that responsibility is shared. A soloist who never listens, or an instrumentalist who drowns the words, has forgotten the group.

### Matching the occasion
If the song is a marriage or naming song, the mood can be joyful. If it is a worship song, the mood is reverent. If it is a work song, the beat should fit the movement. Do not turn a solemn song into a joke.

### Why these songs matter
Folk songs carry language, history and advice. When you sing a song from a community that is not your own, you practise respect and you help keep that song alive. When you sing a song from your own community, you honour the people who taught it. Mocking pronunciation, costume or dance steps is disrespectful. Ask for help, then try again.

Etiquette remains: start together, listen to the soloist, and thank the person who taught you the song. Performing indigenous songs from many Kenyan communities is a way of saying that all those communities belong in the country’s music.

keyWords.meaning: the singer who leads the song
the person who plays the instrument
the part the group sings after the soloist

examples.problem: A class has 1 soloist, 2 instrumentalists and 9 singers. How many performers is that?
The class laughs at the words of a song from another community. What value have they missed?
steps: Folk songs from all Kenyan communities deserve respect.
examples.answer: Respect for indigenous songs and for the community the song comes from.

activity.title: Take a role and perform
steps: Agree the name, community and type of the song.
Share roles: soloist, singers and instrumentalists.
Practise the response until the pitch and the beat are steady.
Perform once for another group, using gestures that fit the occasion.
Swap a role and perform again. Tell the other group one thing you valued in their song.

practice.question: Name three roles in a folk song performance.
practice.answer: Soloist, singers and instrumentalist.

practice.question: What performance techniques should you apply?
practice.answer: Accurate pitch and rhythm, suitable tempo and dynamics, clear diction, and fitting gestures and facial expressions.

practice.question: Why is it valuable to perform songs from different Kenyan communities?
practice.answer: The songs carry language, history and identity, and performing them shows respect for those communities.

summary: Perform with a soloist, singers and an instrumentalist.
Use the techniques and the mood that fit the occasion.
Value indigenous songs from every Kenyan community.

quiz.question: Which song is topical?
quiz.explanation: A topical song is about a theme in daily life, such as hygiene.

quiz.question: What is pitch?
options: How high or low a note is
quiz.explanation: Pitch is the highness or lowness of a note.

quiz.question: Dynamics in music means…
options: how loud or soft the sound is
quiz.explanation: Dynamics are the loudness or softness of the performance.

quiz.question: What is diction?
quiz.explanation: Good diction lets the audience understand the message.

quiz.question: Singing in unison means…
options: each person sings a different tune
everyone sings the same tune at the same time
quiz.explanation: Unison is one shared tune sung together.

quiz.question: What does the first verse of the East African Community Anthem ask for?
quiz.answer: It asks God to guard the Community, and for the people to live in peace and fulfil their aims.
quiz.explanation: Verse 1 is a prayer for protection, peace and fulfilled goals.

quiz.question: A song sung while people grind grain is which type?
quiz.explanation: Songs that accompany shared labour are work songs.

quiz.question: Isukuti is performed especially by which communities?
options: Luhya communities, especially Isukha and Idakho
quiz.explanation: Isukuti is Luhya drum music and dance, well known among the Isukha and Idakho.

quiz.question: Which set names roles in a folk song?
quiz.explanation: A folk song performance uses a soloist, the singers and instrumentalists.

quiz.question: Why should a class value folk songs from communities other than their own?
quiz.answer: Those songs carry language, history and identity, and performing them shows respect.
quiz.explanation: Valuing indigenous songs from many communities builds respect and cultural understanding.

sources: KICD Grade 4 Creative Arts Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 2.0 Performing and Displaying, Sub-strand 2.3 Songs
